idiom_name: hand-written trait implementation in the test module (mockall as optional sugar)
implementation_notes: Traits are the seam: the client is generic over PriceService or takes &dyn PriceService, and a struct in the same file - usually behind #[cfg(test)] - implements the trait, so the compiler proves the stand-in satisfies the contract and no runtime machinery is involved. mockall adds generated doubles when the trait is wide: #[automock] emits MockPriceService with expect_method().returning(...) expectations and panics on calls that contradict them. When the remote is HTTP, wiremock starts a real local server and stands in at the wire level instead of at the trait.
pitfalls: mockall's mocks are always Send, so a trait whose methods take or return non-Send values needs the _st return variants and their runtime access checks.

#[automock] does not cover every shape - structs need a single impl block, and generic methods or impl Trait returns may require the mock! macro; a trait that cannot be doubled is often a design signal.
Storing the double behind Box<dyn PriceService> requires an object-safe trait, so a generic-method trait silently constrains the production design to monomorphised generics.

variants.name: mockall #[automock] generated double with expectations
variants.implementation_notes: Annotating the trait with #[automock] generates a mock struct with typed expectation builders, argument matchers and call counts, and any access contrary to the expectations panics - which is the closest Rust analogue of gMock. Use it for wide traits where hand-writing every method is noise, and keep the hand-written double where the test needs readable canned data.
pitfalls: Every expectation can require a return value and a call count, so a test that forgets .times(0) fails only when the shutdown check runs.
Generated doubles live in the same file as the trait, so the macro must be applied where the trait is visible - re-exported traits need the mock! macro instead.

variants.name: wiremock-rs local server standing in for the HTTP service
variants.idiom_name: MockServer::start with request matchers and response templates
variants.implementation_notes: For HTTP dependencies, wiremock starts a background server on a random local port, matches incoming requests and returns templated responses, and each server is isolated so tests can run in parallel. It exercises the real HTTP client and its error handling, which the trait-level double cannot.
pitfalls: An unmatched request returns 404 rather than failing the test loudly, so a typo in the path looks like a client bug until the assertion reveals it.
Expectations are verified when the server is dropped, so a server kept alive past the end of the test never reports a failed verification.
